*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the harvest of the wicked.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sin.” The term חַטָּאת (khattaʾt, “sin”) functions as a metonymy of cause (= sin) for effect (= punishment). In contrast to the righteous who receive a reward, the wicked receive punishment for their sin (cf. NASB, NIV84, NCV). NIV11 translates “sin and death.” See D. W. Thomas, “The Meaning of חַטָּאת in Proverbs X.16,” *JTS* 15 (1964): 295-96.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “discipline.” The noun מוּסָר (musar) has a basic two-fold range of meanings: (1) “discipline” (so NIV; NAB “admonition”; NCV, NLT “correction”) and (2) “instruction” (BDB 416 s.v.; so KJV, NASB, NRSV). The wise person listens to instruction (first colon); however, the fool will not even take discipline to heart (second colon).

*Translator's note:* The term is a genitive of location indicating the goal (*IBHS* 147-48 §9.5.2f).

*Study note:* The contrast with the one who holds fast to discipline is the one who forsakes or abandons reproof or correction. Whereas the first is an example, this latter individual causes people to wander from the true course of life, that is, causes them to err.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lips of falsehood.” The genitive noun שָׁקֶר (shaqer, “falsehood”) functions as an attributive genitive. The noun “lips” is a metonymy of cause for speech produced by lips. The one who shows friendliness while concealing hatred is a liar (e.g., {{Psalm 28:3|Ps 28:3}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “causes to go out.” The Hiphil of יָצָא (yatsaʾ) literally means “to cause to go out” (BDB 424 s.v. Hiph.1). This may refer to speech (“to utter”) in the sense of causing words to go out of one’s mouth, or it may refer to slander (“to spread”) in the sense of causing slander to go out to others.

*Translator's note:* The word דִבָּה (dibbah) means “whispering; defamation; evil report” (BDB 179 s.v.). Cf. NAB “accusations”; TEV “gossip.”

*Study note:* The one who spreads *slander* is a fool because it not only destroys others but comes back on the guilty. See also the sayings of Amenemope and Ahiqar on these subjects (*ANET* 423, 429).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he is a fool.” The independent personal pronoun הוּא (huʾ, “he”) is used for emphasis. This is reflected in the translation as “certainly.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “does not cease.” It is impossible to avoid sinning in an abundance of words—sooner or later one is bound to say something wrong.

*Translator's note:* Or “holds his lips under control.” The verb חָשַׂךְ (khasakh) means “to withhold; to restrain; to hold in check” (BDB 362 s.v.). The related Arabic term is used in reference to placing a piece of wood in the mouth of a goat to prevent it from sucking (*HALOT* 359 s.v. חשׂךְ).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his lips” (so KJV, NAB, NASB); NIV11 “their tongues.” The term “lips” is a metonymy of cause for speech.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the lips of the righteous.” The term “lips” functions as a metonymy of cause for speech. This contrasts the tongue (metonymy of cause for what they say) with the heart (metonymy of subject for what they intend). What the righteous say is more valuable than what the wicked intend.

*Translator's note:* The comparative “like” is not in the Hebrew text but is implied by the metaphor; it is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity.

*Translator's note:* Or “pure”; *Heb* “choice.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the heart of the wicked” (so KJV, NAB, NIV). The term “heart” functions as a metonymy of cause for thoughts. The term לֵב (lev, “heart”) often refers to the seat of thoughts, will and emotions (BDB 524 s.v. 3-4).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like little.” This expression refers to what has little value: “little worth” (so KJV, NAB, NRSV; cf. BDB 590 s.v. מְעַט 2.d). The point of the metaphor is clarified by the parallelism: Silver is valuable; the heart of the wicked is worth little. *Tg*. {{Proverbs 10:20|Prov 10:20}} says it was full of dross, a contrast with choice silver.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lips.” The term “lips” functions as a metonymy of cause for what is said (or in this case taught).

*Translator's note:* The verb רָעָה (raʿah) means “to feed” or “to shepherd” (e.g., {{Genesis 48:15|Gen 48:15}}). What they say will meet the needs of many.

*Translator's note:* In what sense the fool “dies” is unclear. Fools ruin their lives and the lives of others by their lack of discipline and knowledge. The contrast is between enhancing life and ruining life.

*Translator's note:* The term לֵב (lev, “mind, heart”) is used as a metonymy of association for what one does with the mind (i.e., thinking), and so refers to discernment, wisdom, good sense.

*Translator's note:* The term בְּרָכָה (berakhah, “blessing”) refers to a gift, enrichment or endowment from the Lord.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “of the Lord.” The term יְהוָה (yehvah, “the Lord”) functions here as a genitive of source.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “makes rich” (so NASB); NAB “brings wealth.” The direct object “a person” does not appear in the Hebrew but is implied by the Hiphil verb; it is supplied in the translation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “toil.” The noun עֶצֶב (ʿetsev) has a basic two-fold range of meanings: (1) “toil; labor” which produces pain and sorrow, and (2) “pain; sorrow” which is the result of toil and labor (BDB 780 s.v.). This is the word used of the curse of “toil” in man’s labor ({{Genesis 3:17|Gen 3:17}}) and the “pain” in the woman’s child-bearing ({{Genesis 3:16|Gen 3:16}}). God’s blessing is pure and untarnished—it does not bring physical pain or emotional sorrow.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “doing a plan.” The noun זִמָּה (zimmah, “plan”) is often used pejoratively of a scheme to do wickedness. It is used elsewhere for planning lewdness, murder, incest, adultery, idolatry, and licentiousness. Any planned gross impropriety gives the fool pleasure. The verb עָשָׂה (ʿasah, “to do”) here means “to carry out (a plan)” (BDB 794 s.v.).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like sport” (so NASB, NRSV). The noun שְׂחוֹק (sekhoq, “sport”) is used elsewhere to refer to what is exhilarating and pleasurable (BDB 966 s.v.). As W. G. Plaut says, it is like child’s play (*Proverbs*, 132). For the fool evil brings such enjoyment; for the discerning wisdom does.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a man of discernment.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the dread of the wicked.” The noun רָשָׁע (rashaʿ, “wicked”) is a subjective genitive. The noun מְגוֹרַת (megorat) refers to “the feared thing,” that is, what the wicked dread. The wicked are afraid of the consequences of their sinful actions; however, they cannot escape these consequences.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the desire of the righteous.” The noun צַדִּיק (tsadiq, “righteous”) is a subjective genitive.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it will give.” When used without an expressed subject, the verb יִתֵּן (yitten) has a passive nuance: “it will be granted.”

*Study note:* The word for “storm wind” comes from the root סוּף (suf, “to come to an end; to cease”). The noun may then describe the kind of storm that makes an end of things, a “whirlwind” (so KJV, NASB; NLT “cyclone”). It is used in prophetic passages that describe swift judgment and destruction.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the wicked are not”; ASV, NAB, NASB “is no more.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a foundation forever”; NLT “have a lasting foundation.”

*Study note:* The metaphor compares the righteous to an everlasting foundation to stress that they are secure when the catastrophes of life come along. He is fixed in a covenantal relationship and needs not to fear passing misfortunes. The wicked has no such security.

*Study note:* Two similes are used to portray the aggravation in sending a lazy person to accomplish a task. Vinegar to the teeth is an unpleasant, irritating experience; and smoke to the eyes is an unpleasant experience that hinders progress.

*Translator's note:* The participle is plural, and so probably should be taken in a distributive sense: “to each one who sends him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the fear of the Lord.” The term יְהוָה (yehvah, “the Lord”) functions as an objective genitive.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “days” (so KJV, ASV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “years.” The term “years” functions as a synecdoche of part (= years) for the whole (= lifespan).

*Study note:* This general saying has to be qualified with the problem of the righteous suffering and dying young, a problem that perplexed the sages of the entire ancient world. But this is the general principle: The righteous live longer because their life is the natural one and because God blesses them.

*Study note:* This proverb contrasts the hopes of the righteous and the wicked. The righteous will see their hopes fulfilled. The saying is concerned with God’s justice. The words תּוֹחֶלֶת (tokhelet, from יָחַל, yakhal) and תִּקְוַת (tiqvat, from קָוָה, qavah) are synonyms, both emphasizing eager expectations, longings, waiting in hope.

*Study note:* The “way of the Lord” is an idiom for God’s providential administration of life; it is what the Lord does (“way” being a hypocatastasis).

*Text-critical note:* The LXX reads “the fear of the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* The comparative “like” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is implied by the metaphor; it is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “for the one with integrity” (לַתֹּם, lattom). The versions appear to read לְתַם (letam) “for the blameless.”

*Translator's note:* Or “ruin” (so NIV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who practice iniquity.”

*Study note:* This proverb concerns the enjoyment of covenant blessings—dwelling in the land of Israel. It is promised to the righteous for an eternal inheritance, and so the wicked cannot expect to settle there—they will be exiled.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the mouth.” The term פֶּה (peh, “mouth”) functions as a metonymy of cause for speech.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bears wisdom.” The verb נוּב (nuv) means “to bear fruit.” It is used figuratively of the righteous; they produce wisdom and righteousness. The term חָכְמָה (khokhmah, “wisdom”) represents the “fruit” that the righteous bear: “they bear the fruit of wisdom” (BDB 626 s.v.).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the tongue of perversions.” The noun תַּהְפֻּכוֹת (tahpukhot, “perversions”) functions as a genitive of content; it refers to what the tongue says—perverse things. The plural form depicts a plural of character. The term לָשׁוֹן (lashon, “tongue”) functions as a synecdoche of part (= tongue) for the whole person (= the speaker). The tongue is emphasized because this person is characterized by perverse speech. The term תַּהְפֻּכוֹת (“perversions”) refers to those who turn things upside down, overthrow, or pervert what is right.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will be cut off” (so NAB, NRSV, NLT); cf. KJV, NASB, NIV84 “cut out”; NIV11 “be silenced.” Their tongue will be cut off, a hyperbole meaning to bring to an end the evil that they speak.

*Study note:* The verb “know” applied to “lips” is unusual. “Lips” is a metonymy for what the righteous say; and their words “know” (a personification) what is pleasing, i.e., they are acquainted with.

*Study note:* The righteous say what is pleasing, acceptable, or delightful, but the wicked say perverse and destructive things.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lips.” The term “lips” is a metonymy of cause for what is said.
